show: Princess Story (musical staged at Auditorio Municipal Paco de Lucía, Alcalá de Henares)
synopsis:
Songs begin to ring out as a succession of beloved princesses steps into the light, opening the doors to the fairy-tale worlds that have shaped their dreams. Each heroine takes her turn at centre stage to share the moments that tested her courage: wishes made in loneliness, journeys into unfamiliar places, encounters with danger, and the determination to choose her own path rather than surrender to fear. Through live musical numbers, dancing, and playful theatrical scenes, their separate adventures unfold as a colourful procession of romance, friendship, magic, and hard-won confidence.

The princesses move between moments of celebration and uncertainty, showing that royal gowns and enchanted settings do not spare them from difficult choices. Some must trust strangers, some must stand up to those who would control them, and others must discover that the answer they seek lies in their own voice, loyalty, or imagination. Familiar songs carry the action from one storybook realm to another, while the performers invite the audience to share in the excitement, laughter, and emotional turns of each tale.

As the stories gather momentum, the stage becomes a meeting place for heroines whose experiences differ but whose hopes are alike. Their songs affirm that a dream can survive obstacles when it is matched by kindness, bravery, and the willingness to act. The final celebration brings the princesses together in a joyful affirmation of the magic created when stories are sung, remembered, and shared. After the performance, the audience is invited to meet the princesses in person, extending the fantasy beyond the final number.

The show celebrates courage, self-belief, friendship, and the sustaining power of dreams. It treats fairy tales as a shared space in which children and adults can find wonder, emotional reassurance, and permission to imagine a brighter future.

show: ¡Bienvenidos! Un musical con éxitos de los 80's y 90's (musical staged at Auditorio Municipal Paco de Lucía, Alcalá de Henares)
synopsis:
Blanca leaves her pueblo behind and arrives in Madrid carrying a fierce love of music and a determination to escape the pressure imposed by her father. The city’s vibrant Movida Madrileña promises freedom, noise and possibility, but its streets also force her to confront the uncertainty behind her dream. As she searches for a place where her talent can be heard, Blanca encounters new voices and restless young people who, like her, are trying to become someone beyond the expectations and pain that have shaped them.

Three young people gradually become her closest companions and the family she has chosen for herself. Bound by music, late-night hopes and the desire to make a future in the city, they find encouragement in one another’s ambitions. Yet their shared adventure is not simply a release from the past: each carries fears, vulnerabilities and addictions that threaten to pull the group apart. Blanca’s arrival unsettles old routines and gives the others a reason to imagine a different life, while their struggles reveal that running away does not automatically erase what hurts.

Together, they pursue the exhilaration of performing, discovering talent in unexpected places and turning the music around them into a language of friendship and survival. Their relationships are tested as private conflicts surface, dreams collide with hard realities, and the promise of Madrid becomes more complicated than Blanca first imagined. To remain together, they must decide whether they can face their fears honestly rather than hide behind celebration, rebellion or escape. Through setbacks and renewed determination, they learn to protect the hopes that first brought them together.

The musical celebrates friendship, self-discovery and the sustaining power of music in moments of uncertainty. It also argues that dreams matter most when people have the courage to confront fear, pain and dependency rather than abandon one another.

show: Encantats (musical staged at Kinepolis Full (Splau), Cornellà de Llobregat, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Martí barely looks up from his screen when he is sent away for the summer to the village where his brother, Miquel, lives with Miquel’s wife, Maria del Mar. To the teenager, the arrangement feels like a punishment: he has been removed from his habitual digital refuge and deposited in a place whose slower rhythms, familiar faces and local customs seem impossible to take seriously. Miquel and Maria del Mar must find a way to live with Martí’s impatience and disengagement, while the village watches the newcomer with keen curiosity.

As the days unfold, Martí’s unwanted stay slips beyond the ordinary. Legends once treated as old stories begin to feel present, and the village becomes a landscape of fantasy inhabited by fades, strange surprises and veïnes tafaneres who miss nothing and comment on everything. Humour grows out of the collision between Martí’s screen-bound outlook and a community that insists on drawing him into its conversations, memories and eccentricities. What begins as an awkward family summer develops into an unpredictable adventure, in which the border between everyday village life and the fabulous becomes increasingly porous.

Caught up in this peculiar world, Martí has to confront the distance between being endlessly connected and genuinely participating in the lives around him. His encounters with the village’s magical and meddlesome inhabitants gradually make room for new forms of attention: to Miquel and Maria del Mar, to the people who have made a shared life there, and to his own need to be noticed. The summer that he expected merely to endure becomes a chance for reunion, laughter and emotional openness.

Built on more than thirty hits of Catalan pop-rock, the show turns that shared songbook into a space of collective memory, and celebrates connection—within families, among neighbours and through the music a whole audience already carries. It contrasts the isolation of screens with the vulnerable but restorative act of being seen, loved and heard.

show: A media luz (musical staged at Espacio Alma, Madrid)
synopsis:
A tango for three bodies and a city. In the half-light, three people move through a shared night carrying desires they have not yet dared to name aloud, in an openly LGBTIQ+ story about love, freedom and the bonds between people. Their lives are about to intersect, drawn together by music, chance encounters and the private longings that each has tried to contain. In a world where every tango seems to hold a secret, attraction becomes both an invitation and a threat: the more closely they come to one another, the harder it is to preserve the reassuring stories they tell themselves.

As the connections among the three deepen, affection refuses to fit into a simple, exclusive shape. Each person must confront not merely whom they desire, but what honesty requires when that desire reaches beyond a conventional couple. Silence, evasion and fear of causing pain turn intimacy into a delicate negotiation. A glance, a dance and an unfinished confession acquire the weight of decisions, while the city surrounding them becomes a fourth presence—watching, sheltering and reflecting their changing emotional landscape.

The tension does not arise from the existence of love for two people, but from the uncertainty of how to sustain it without deceit, possessiveness or self-erasure. The three are forced to ask whether freedom can be lived responsibly, whether vulnerability can replace control, and whether they can meet one another as they truly are. Tango gives form to what speech cannot easily resolve: desire, jealousy, tenderness, hesitation and the hope that honesty may lead not to abandonment, but to a more generous way of being together.

At its heart, A Media Luz considers love as an act of truthfulness rather than a matter of labels or fixed rules. It explores freedom, queer intimacy and human bonds, asking how people can love openly without betraying either themselves or those closest to them.

show: A Todo Ritmo (musical staged at Espacio Broadway (Madrid), Madrid)
synopsis:
Aitana throws herself into life with the assurance of a woman who knows her own mind, while Reta arrives as a romantic calamity: impulsive, tender, and forever arranging his feelings into the soundtrack of a playlist. Their attraction is immediate, but neither of them is equipped to make love simple. In a succession of encounters, misunderstandings, break-ups, and improbable reunions, the pair collide with the force of two people who cannot quite stay together and cannot quite let each other go.

Their story moves through changing eras and moods, travelling from the pop-inflected memories of the 1960s to the energy of present-day parties. A shared Fanta, a song that catches them off guard, a dance that becomes too charged to dismiss, and the aftermath of a broken heart all become turning points in their uneven relationship. Aitana’s independence repeatedly clashes with Reta’s grand, often ill-judged romantic instincts; his attempts to win her back can be as ridiculous as they are sincere. As the years and musical styles shift around them, each new meeting tests whether they have learned anything from the last goodbye.

Comedy erupts from the absurdity of their emotional habits: declarations made at the worst possible moment, jealous impulses, nostalgia sharpened by pop songs, and the modern temptation to block someone only to keep watching from a distance. Yet beneath the chaos, their connection remains recognisable. Every reconciliation carries the possibility of another mistake, while every separation leaves behind the question of whether imperfect love can still be real love.

The musical celebrates love as messy, irrational, and sometimes painfully funny rather than neat or idealised. Through nostalgia, dancing, and pop-driven emotional memory, it suggests that people may not solve love’s contradictions—but they can choose to keep moving to its rhythm.

show: Alicia en el país de las maravillas (musical staged at Teatro Lara, Madrid)
synopsis:
Alicia’s longing for something beyond the ordinary takes shape when she meets the Sr. Conejo, who leads her into a dazzling, unpredictable realm where dreams seem able to come true. Eager to embrace every surprise, she leaves familiar certainties behind and begins a journey governed by imagination rather than sensible rules.

Her path brings her face to face with the Oruga Azul and the elusive Gatita de Cheshire, whose appearances turn each new encounter into another test of Alicia’s curiosity and courage. Rather than retreating from the strangeness around her, Alicia presses on, finding wonder in a world whose inhabitants and customs continually overturn what she expects.

The journey becomes a celebration at the Sombrerero Loco’s NO CUMPLEAÑOS, where Alicia shares the occasion with Humpty Dumpty. What should be an ordinary gathering becomes a playful, topsy-turvy festivity, confirming that this is a place in which the everyday can be remade through games, laughter, and fantasy.

At last, Alicia reaches the Gran Torneo de Croquet and faces the formidable Reina de Corazones. The contest provides the adventure’s grand climax: amid the Queen’s authority and the heightened excitement of the game, Alicia must draw on everything she has discovered during her extraordinary passage through this magical country.

The musical celebrates imagination as a force that opens hidden possibilities and transforms the familiar into adventure. It also presents curiosity, playfulness, and the willingness to meet the unknown as qualities that help Alicia navigate a world where rules can change at any moment.

show: Armstrong, un musical muy espacial (musical staged at Teatro Sanpol, Madrid)
synopsis:
Piper studies hard at the Instituto de Aeronáutica Espacial, carrying with her the stories she has heard all her life about her grandfather, Neil Armstrong, the first person to set foot on the Moon. Those memories have turned her own wish to fly into a determined ambition: she wants to become an astronaut and follow a path that seems, quite literally, written among the stars. Her opportunity arrives when the school prepares the launch of Misión Apolo 18, an expedition intended to return human beings to the lunar surface.

The mission is fiercely competitive. Only three students will earn a place aboard the rocket, so Piper must face a series of demanding tests to prove that she has the skill, courage, and perseverance required for space travel. Each obstacle brings the launch closer while forcing her to measure herself against the challenge of reaching the Moon—and against the fear that she may not be chosen.

Yet the danger does not come only from the selection process. A group of malicious hackers plans to sabotage Misión Apolo 18. Their goal is to reach the Moon before the students, steal its lunar rocks, and become rich from them. As their scheme threatens both the expedition and Piper’s dream, the young candidates must confront a mystery that turns their academic challenge into an urgent adventure. Piper cannot succeed through individual effort alone: protecting the mission requires trust, friendship, and the ability to work together when the countdown has already begun.

At its heart, the show celebrates perseverance, friendship, and teamwork in the face of a seemingly impossible goal. It also treats Piper’s bond with her grandfather, Neil Armstrong, as an affectionate tribute to grandparents and to the dreams they inspire across generations.

show: Artemis (musical staged at Teatre Condal, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Diana escapes into science fiction whenever life on Earth becomes too painful to bear. Still carrying the wound of her father’s disappearance in childhood, she idealises the absent figure while feeling increasingly unable to reach her mother, whose practical outlook clashes with Diana’s restless imagination. Cinema becomes Diana’s shelter: she studies the worlds it creates and becomes fixated on writing a science-fiction screenplay of her own — film is the one field she wants to work in, though film schools cost far more than she can reach — and treats the unfamiliar territory of adolescence as though she were an astronaut preparing for a hostile expedition.

Having changed schools to leave the conflicts of the last one behind, and finding it hard to make friends, Diana must navigate a new social universe and the frightening possibility of being seen for who she really is. First love arrives with all the intensity of one of her beloved films, yet the longing to be wanted feeds her fear of rejection. Clever and quick-witted, she discovers that embellishing the truth wins attention and affection. What begins as a tactic becomes compulsive: each lie offers a brief escape from loneliness, but pushes her further from the people who might genuinely know and support her, and the spiral of lies she builds will eventually present its bill.

As fantasy, memory and everyday life blur, Diana cannot stay forever in the protective orbit of invented stories, nor keep avoiding the grief and anger around her father’s absence. Growing up means facing the most daunting encounter of all: an honest confrontation with her mother. Their conflict reveals a shared trauma within a single-parent family, and forces Diana to decide whether she can exchange idealised illusions for a more difficult, compassionate relationship with the past and with herself.

At its core, Artemis is about loneliness, family rupture and the perilous comfort of fantasy, arguing that maturity begins when Diana faces the truth, takes responsibility for her choices, and makes room for reconciliation, creativity and mental wellbeing.

show: Assassinat per a dos (musical staged at Teatre Goya, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Arthur Whitney lies murdered in the drawing room of his own home, and Officer Marcus Moscowitz sees the crime as his long-awaited chance to become a real detective. Determined to prove that his instincts are as sharp as any seasoned investigator’s, Marcus takes charge of the scene and begins hunting for the killer before the trail grows cold. The difficulty is immediate: Whitney has left behind not one obvious culprit, but twelve possible suspects — all of them, and Marcus besides, played by just two actors who between them cover thirteen roles and take turns at the piano, each with a reason to be questioned and a story that may conceal more than it reveals.

Marcus turns his attention to the people closest to the dead novelist. Dahlía, Arthur’s widow, must account for her place in the household and her relationship with the victim. Dr. Griff, Arthur’s psychologist, brings the unsettling possibility that private knowledge of the writer’s mind may have turned dangerous. Paulette Lewis, a celebrated dancer, enters the investigation with her own connection to the murdered man. Even the unbearable neighbours, Harry and Anne, become entangled in the web of suspicion. As Marcus moves from one interrogation to the next, every answer creates fresh doubts, every personality seems capable of deception, and the case becomes an increasingly frantic race to identify the murderer.

With barely more than an hour to crack the mystery, Marcus must sort through conflicting accounts, shifting motives and a crowded gallery of eccentric suspects. His dream of becoming a detective depends on finding the truth hidden amid the confusion—before the investigation, and his hard-won opportunity, slips beyond his control.

The show turns the machinery of a classic whodunnit into a comic examination of ambition, appearances and misdirection. It celebrates the pleasure of suspicion: anyone may be guilty, every clue may mislead, and certainty must be earned through persistence.

show: ¡Bienvenidos! Un musical con los éxitos de los 80's y los 90's-Totana (musical staged at Teatro Ginés Rosa, Totana)
synopsis:
Blanca leaves her village behind, fleeing both the narrow future laid out for her and her father’s pressure to abandon the one thing she cannot silence: her passion for music. She arrives in Madrid during the years of the Movida Madrileña, carrying more hope than certainty and searching for a place where she can be heard. The city is noisy, restless and full of possibility; in its streets, bars and musical corners, Blanca discovers performers whose energy and talent turn every encounter into an invitation to risk more.

As she finds her way through this new world, Blanca meets three young people who become far more than casual companions. Drawn together by music, ambition and the need to belong, they form a chosen family in a city that can be both exhilarating and unforgiving. Yet each of them carries private struggles. Fear shadows their boldest plans, while addiction and self-doubt threaten to pull them away from one another and from the futures they imagine.

Their shared journey forces them to confront what they are running from as well as what they hope to gain. Blanca must decide whether pursuing a dream means cutting herself off from her past, while her new friends learn that talent alone cannot protect them from the consequences of their choices. Through moments of celebration, conflict and renewed determination, the group discovers that dreams must be defended—not only when life seems full of open doors, but especially when hope feels most fragile.

At its heart, the musical celebrates friendship, self-expression and the courage to pursue a life of one’s own. It also reflects on fear, addiction and the sustaining power of dreams when people face uncertainty together.

show: Busco pis! (musical staged at Teatre Apolo, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
At the opening of the BCN Sell&Rent Village, the city’s most important real-estate convention, major landlords gather to protect their share of the housing business. Laia is nowhere near the event. At thirty-six, she is still living with her parents, painfully removed from the world of investment portfolios, property deals and people who treat homes as assets. What she wants is far more basic: a place of her own and the independence that ought to come with it. Yet finding a flat has become so difficult that every attempt seems to lead to another closed door.

Driven by desperation, Laia makes one last push to escape her situation—and is drawn into an escalating mess that takes her straight through the strange ecosystem surrounding the housing market. Her search exposes her to agents in green ties, large-scale property owners who cry, foreign newcomers—guiris—eating avocado toast, and politicians who seem chiefly interested in appearing for the photograph. As Laia moves among these figures, the line between ordinary people looking for somewhere to live and those who profit from scarcity becomes increasingly stark. The forces shaping her life turn out to be theatrical, absurd and relentlessly self-serving, while her private wish for a home collides with a city-wide commercial spectacle.

The musical turns the housing crisis into a biting comic landscape, using exaggeration and farce to expose the interests behind it. Its central themes are precarity, inequality and the struggle to preserve dignity when a basic need becomes a commodity.

show: Chuchuwá viaja jugando (musical staged at Espacio Alma, Madrid)
synopsis:
Ali, Popy and Nina arrive at the estación ready to begin a joyous journey aboard the magical train Chuchuwá, inviting the young passengers around them to make the adventure move forward with songs, gestures and play. Their companion Tulo is meant to travel with them, but the group soon needs everyone’s help to find him, call the train and turn each new stop into a shared game. Rather than remaining quietly in their seats, the children join the expedition as active passengers: they sing, dance, copy movements and answer the characters’ calls as the train crosses from one imagined world to the next.

The first destination opens onto the selva, where the travellers use animal sounds and imitations to explore their unfamiliar surroundings. Each encounter becomes a cue for a musical number and a playful challenge, allowing Ali, Popy and Nina to transform the search for Tulo into a cooperative mission. When the train reaches the granja, the group continues the game through familiar children’s songs, including “La Vaca Lola,” “Soy una taza,” “El Pollito Pío” and “Cabeza, hombros, rodillas y pies.” Singing and choreography give the passengers ways to participate directly, whether by moving their bodies, following rhythms or helping the characters complete a task.

The journey finally carries them toward the arcoíris, a bright, imaginative space in which the separate stops feel like parts of one larger adventure. By travelling together, playing at every station and supporting the search, Ali, Popy, Nina, Tulo and their fellow passengers turn the train ride into a celebration of collective make-believe.

At its heart, the show celebrates friendship, teamwork and the pleasure of taking part rather than simply watching. It also encourages empathy and a playful respect for the natural world, using music and movement to make shared imagination the vehicle of the journey.

show: Cinderela - O Musical (musical staged at Europarque, Aveiro, Portuguese-language production)
synopsis:
At home, Cinderela endures the daily cruelty of her Madrasta and her two daughters, who treat her as a servant while she quietly holds on to the hope that life can change. Though surrounded by scorn and impossible demands, she refuses to let bitterness define her, trusting that her dreams may yet lead her toward happiness.

When the chance arises to leave behind the household’s hardships and enter a world beyond its walls, Cinderela’s longing seems destined to remain out of reach. Then her Fada Madrinha appears, bringing magic at the moment when Cinderela most needs courage. With her help, the young woman is transformed for a night of wonder, but the gift comes with a condition: she must return before the enchantment ends.

Away from the control of her Madrasta and stepsisters, Cinderela is finally able to show the kindness, grace, and hope that have survived every humiliation. Yet the happiness she finds is threatened by the passing hours. As midnight approaches, she must flee, leaving behind the proof of a life briefly made possible by faith and imagination. What remains sets in motion the search that can reunite her with the future she has always dared to believe in. Through magic, music, and dance, Cinderela’s perseverance carries her from oppression toward the possibility of love, recognition, and a different life.

The musical celebrates the conviction that dreams require belief as well as courage. It presents kindness, respect for others, hope, and faith in the future as forces capable of overcoming adversity.

show: Crush (musical staged at Teatre Akadèmia, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Eva and Marc mark their fourth anniversary together, carrying into the evening both the happiness of their shared life and all that neither has quite managed to say. Eva, a neuroscientist, and Marc, a musician, have made parenthood part of the future they imagine together; yet the wish to have a child, so easy to name, has proved far harder to inhabit. As they celebrate, conversation exposes the strain between what they have planned, what they fear, and what each of them needs in the present.

Their night becomes a space in which words, songs, and physical closeness attempt to bridge what silence has left unresolved. The couple confronts the expectations attached to fertility, motherhood, and fatherhood, along with the private pressure of measuring a relationship against an anticipated next step. They must reckon with whether their desire for a family still belongs to them as they are now, or whether it has been shaped by inherited ideas of what a successful life and partnership should look like.

Then comes a brief, decisive pause: an instant in which time seems to stop. In the void opened by that silence, Eva and Marc are forced to look at the distance between their carefully imagined future and the emotional reality before them. What has been withheld begins to matter as much as what has been spoken, and their anniversary becomes an encounter with the fragility of their bond, the uncertain paths toward—or away from—parenthood, and the possibility that life can change before either person has found the language for it.

At its heart, the musical considers love under pressure: the collision of desire, expectation, and the limits of time. It asks whether people can pause long enough to face grief, joy, uncertainty, and one another honestly, rather than simply moving toward the next expected milestone.

show: Després de nosaltres (musical staged at Espai Texas, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
A year after their breakup, Lena goes to see Adrià, determined not to let the person who once mattered most to her vanish from her life. They are no longer a couple, yet neither can honestly call what remains unimportant. Adrià, a film-score composer absorbed by a demanding new commission, has tried to rebuild a calmer, more self-contained life; Lena, who works for a prestigious music festival, arrives carrying her own uncertainties and a wish to restore the closeness they promised each other they would preserve.

Their reunion forces them to confront an arrangement for which neither has a model: being present for one another without returning to the relationship they had. Old ease and shared humour resurface, but so do the habits, expectations and emotions that made their separation necessary. Each encounter tests the boundary between friendship and unfinished love, especially when private difficulties make the other seem like the most natural person to call. The question becomes not whether they can remain in contact, but what kind of contact will allow both of them to grow rather than keep them trapped in the past.

As changes in work, city and daily life reshape their separate paths, Lena and Adrià try to keep their bond alive without pretending that nothing has changed. The prospect of new partners raises further complications: can they offer each other care without making space for new lives impossible? Their attempts to answer that question move between tenderness, comic awkwardness and the sting of recognising that love can endure even after a romantic relationship has ended.

The musical centres on love after separation: not its disappearance, but its difficult transformation. It asks whether affection, loyalty and mutual care can survive once a couple must learn to become something else.

show: Divorcio igualitario (musical staged at Teatro Lara - Sala Lola Membrives, Madrid)
synopsis:
Raúl and Moisés sit down to sign the papers that formally end their marriage. From that painful, apparently final moment, their story moves backwards: each scene peels away a later layer of hurt to reveal the arguments, reconciliations, shared habits, private jokes, disappointments and tender gestures that shaped their life together. The separation is never treated as an isolated catastrophe; it is the outcome of a relationship that was once entered with conviction, desire and the hope that love could hold everything else in place.

As time rewinds, moments of distance give way to periods of complicity. Conflicts that seem definitive are followed—in the reverse chronology—by attempts to repair them; the weariness of routine yields to the excitement of discovering a life together. Raúl and Moisés confront the ordinary pressures that can unsettle even a devoted couple: incompatible expectations, emotional misunderstandings, domestic friction, vulnerability and the difficulty of remaining close when affection begins to coexist with resentment. Songs and intimate encounters turn the backward journey into an emotional reconstruction, allowing what has been lost to be seen alongside what was genuinely built.

Knowing from the outset that their marriage will dissolve changes the meaning of every earlier episode. A reconciliation carries the shadow of the rupture to come, while a disagreement becomes part of a longer process rather than a single decisive wound. Yet the further the story travels toward its beginning, the more clearly it restores the couple’s openness to possibility. The final destination is their wedding day: not an ending made triumphant by ignorance, but the radiant first step of two men choosing each other wholeheartedly despite everything the audience has already witnessed.

At its core, the musical considers how love can be real and profound even when it does not last forever. It treats marriage, separation, memory and regret as shared human experiences, insisting that the emotional patterns of love and heartbreak are not defined by the genders of the people who live them.

show: El Alma al aire (musical staged at Teatro OCASO Coliseum, Madrid)
synopsis:
Ale, a gifted young musician, lives in a small fishing village where the rhythms of work, family and old customs are carried on the wind off the sea. At the heart of the community stands an old railway carriage converted into a bar, a meeting place where memories resurface, quarrels flare and generations cross paths. Ale shares the unsettled hopes of those around him, including his close friend Bruno, while the bonds within his own family pull him between loyalty to the place that formed him and the possibility of a different future.

That precarious balance is disrupted when Alma arrives from Madrid. A real-estate developer, she settles in the village with her two daughters, bringing plans, expectations and a way of life that challenges the community’s long-established order. Her presence touches every relationship: private desires emerge, friendships are tested and people who have grown accustomed to silence must decide what they are prepared to lose, protect or change. Ale and Bruno are caught in the shifting currents created by the newcomers, as affection, ambition and the desire to belong make simple choices impossible.

Around them, the village becomes a space where the everyday takes on an almost magical charge. The wind appears to carry voices, music and long-buried feelings; encounters that seem accidental expose the connections between people; and the old bar becomes a refuge for confession as well as confrontation. As the characters face turning points that may define their futures, Ale must reckon with his talent, his attachments and the life he wants to build, while Alma’s arrival forces the whole village to confront whether its roots can survive without becoming a prison.

The musical centres on the pull of home, friendship and family, and on the courage required to embrace change without denying one’s past. It treats music and the almost magical power the village attributes to the south wind as forces that reconnect people with feeling, memory and the urgency of truly living.

show: El fil invisible (musical staged at Teatre Goya, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Míriam, a writer searching for the right idea for a very special story, begins to imagine Nura, a girl who discovers a remarkable secret hidden in her belly button: an invisible thread. Though no one can see or touch it, the thread reaches from Nura to the people she loves, crossing distance and remaining present even when someone is absent. The discovery gives Nura a new way to understand the warmth and reassurance of her closest relationships.

When her classmate Àlex loses his smile, Nura refuses to let him face his sadness alone. She turns to her friends Quim and Lia, and the three set out with Àlex on an imaginative, playful adventure to help him find what has gone missing. Along the way, Nura shares the secret of the invisible thread and invites the others to recognise the connections in their own lives. Quim and Lia bring their different ways of seeing the world to the journey, while Àlex gradually finds room to express what he feels rather than simply hiding it behind silence.

Their search does not depend on a single magical object or an easy solution. Instead, the children learn that love can remain close when families and friends are apart, and that remembering the people who care for them can offer courage during loneliness, uncertainty, and grief. As Míriam’s imagined tale takes shape, Nura and her friends discover that the unseen bonds between people can be felt most strongly when they choose to look after one another.

The musical celebrates affection, friendship, and the enduring emotional ties that connect people across time and space. It also treats sadness and absence with gentleness, suggesting that connection can provide comfort without making difficult feelings disappear.

show: El flautista de Hamelin (musical staged at Teatro Fígaro, Madrid)
synopsis:
Rats pour through the streets of Hamelín, turning ordinary life upside down as the town’s adults struggle helplessly to stop the infestation. With every attempt failing and desperation mounting, an unfamiliar flautista arrives and offers a solution: in return for the reward the inhabitants promise him, he will rid Hamelín of the plague. His flute begins to sound, and its hypnotic melody draws the rats away. The impossible seems to have happened—Hamelín is saved, and its people can finally breathe again.

But relief soon exposes the adults’ ingratitude. Having regained their clean streets and safety, the inhabitants refuse to honour the payment they pledged to the flautista. Their decision dismisses both the value of his work and the word they gave when they needed him most. Rejected and unpaid, he returns to his flute, transforming the same musical power that rescued the town into an unsettling summons.

This time it is not the rats who answer the melody. It is the children of Hamelín who hear it and recognise in it something the adults no longer can, and the town is forced to face what its broken promise has set in motion. From here the production parts company with the tale as it is usually told: rather than closing on the ending everyone expects, it builds one of its own, shaped by what the children perceive and by what they choose for themselves.

The musical considers promises, justice, and the moral cost of greed, asking what happens when adults treat trust as expendable. It also places childhood, imagination, and art at its centre, suggesting that children may perceive possibilities and injustices that the adult world has forgotten how to see.

show: El Hilo Invisible (musical staged at Teatro Alcázar, Madrid)
synopsis:
Míriam sits before a blank page, searching for the spark that will let her write a very special story. As her imagination takes shape, it leads her to Nura, a girl who discovers an extraordinary secret hidden in her navel: an invisible thread that links her to the people she loves, regardless of distance or time. What first seems like a private wonder becomes a way of seeing the unseen bonds that remain present even when loved ones cannot be nearby.

Nura shares her discovery with her friends Quimi and Lia, and their everyday world soon becomes the starting point for an adventure. Their classmate Álex has lost his smile, and the three friends resolve to help him find it again. Guided by Nura’s new understanding of the hilo invisible, they set out together in search of whatever may ease Álex’s sadness. Along the way, Nura, Quimi, Lia, and Álex confront feelings that are not always easy to name: loneliness, worry, affection, and the need to know that someone is there for them.

The journey does not depend on a single magical solution. Instead, each step teaches the children that care can travel beyond what is visible, and that friendship is strengthened through attention, imagination, and the willingness to stay close to another person’s emotions. As Álex’s lost smile gradually becomes possible again, Nura comes to understand that the thread is not something to hold in one’s hand, but something felt in the connections between people. Míriam’s act of writing and Nura’s adventure ultimately meet in the same shared tale.

The musical centres on invisible emotional bonds: those of family, friendship, and enduring affection across absence and distance. It suggests that recognising these connections can help people face sadness, offer comfort, and feel less alone.

show: El ladrón de Arabia (musical staged at Palacio de Congresos de Plasencia, Plasencia)
synopsis:
Ágrabah is a land where anything is possible — including a princess falling in love with someone from the poorest streets of the city, breaking the rules that are meant to keep the two of them apart and crossing the social barriers built between them. The story is told by the one figure who has watched it all from inside the lamp: the genio. He is the show’s narrator and, by the company’s own account, its real protagonist, and it is through him that the audience is led into Ágrabah.

At the centre of that world is Jasmine. The fight to choose whom she loves, and the fight to be treated as an equal, are both embodied in her, and the production puts that struggle underneath everything else it stages. Aladdín, the humble young man she is not supposed to want, is given a single objective the genio keeps returning to: to follow true love wherever it leads him. The lámpara maravillosa is the ground the story stands on rather than the point of it, and the genio emerges from it to help Aladdín reach what he is after.

Rather than restaging the tale as a conventional book musical, the company presents it as a tribute — told through the genio in a way, they claim, it has never been told before. Broadway numbers never previously sung in Spain sit alongside the songs everyone already knows, among them “el genio tan genial” and “un mundo ideal”. Live voices, costumes drawn from the palaces of the East, and choreography that pays open homage to Bollywood carry the telling.

At its heart the show argues that love should not be dictated by rank or protocol, and that the person with the least power in a kingdom may be the one who changes what is possible in it.

show: El Libro de la Selva, La Aventura de Mowgli (musical staged at Teatro Tepeyac, México, Mexican production)
synopsis:
Mowgli races through the selva with the Lobos who rescued him as a baby, believing their pack is the only family he needs. Bagheera, the wise pantera who has watched over him, knows that danger is closing in: Shere Khan, the feared tigre, despises humankind and has sworn vengeance after humans destroyed his family. Convinced that Mowgli cannot remain safe among the animals, Bagheera insists on taking him to the aldea del hombre, even when the boy resists leaving the life he knows.

Their journey becomes a succession of tempting detours and hard lessons. Mowgli encounters the flamboyant Rey Louie, whose grand manner and strange promises draw him further from Bagheera’s urgent mission. He must also face Kaa, a serpiente whose hypnotic presence turns curiosity into peril. Yet the deepest challenge comes when Mowgli meets Baloo, an affectionate, carefree oso who lives by enjoying the moment. Baloo welcomes the boy warmly and soon treats him like a son, offering him a joyful alternative to the uncertain future Bagheera has chosen for him.

Caught between Bagheera’s responsibility, Baloo’s love, and his own longing to belong, Mowgli has to grow beyond the safety of childhood. As Shere Khan’s threat becomes unavoidable, the friends’ separate paths converge, and Mowgli must find the courage to face the enemy who sees him only as a human intruder. The road toward the aldea del hombre becomes not merely an escape, but a test of where Mowgli truly belongs.

The musical celebrates friendship, chosen family, and the care that can take different forms: Bagheera protects through duty, while Baloo protects through affection. It also frames growing up as the difficult process of accepting change without losing the bonds and lessons that made one strong.

show: El Mago de Oz (musical staged at Teatro Sanpol, Madrid)
synopsis:
A tornado lifts Dorita and her faithful dog Toto from their home in Kansas and drops them into the dazzling, unfamiliar land of Oz. There she discovers a world shaped by magic, where benevolent and threatening forces coexist and the Bruja del Oeste watches her every move. Longing to get home again, Dorita is told that the mysterious Mago de Oz may be able to help her—if she can reach him by following the camino de baldosas amarillas.

On the journey, Dorita and Toto are joined by three companions with wishes of their own. The Espantapájaros believes he lacks a brain; the Hombre de Hojalata mourns the absence of a heart; and the timid León is convinced that he has no courage. Bound by their shared hope, the four travellers press onward through strange, enchanted landscapes, encouraging one another whenever fear, uncertainty, or the Bruja del Oeste threatens to stop them. Each obstacle tests the qualities they believe they do not possess: the Espantapájaros must think, the Hombre de Hojalata must feel, and the León must face danger despite his terror.

At last, they arrive in Oz to seek an audience with its formidable ruler. Yet the solution to their desires proves less simple than they expect, and the friends must confront the Bruja del Oeste before their journey can truly end. Dorita’s greatest wish remains the same throughout: to find her way home with Toto, to the place she now understands more deeply than ever.

The musical celebrates friendship, perseverance, and the strength that emerges when people support one another. It also suggests that intelligence, compassion, courage, and a sense of home may already exist within us, waiting to be recognised.

show: El Misterio de Chamberí (musical staged at Espacio Alma, Madrid)
synopsis:
The doors of Madrid’s newly inaugurated Metropolitano open on 31 October 1919, and a jubilant musical celebration ushers passengers into the promise of a new age. Inside the Metro de Madrid, amid the excitement of its first day, a doctor from 1919 is drawn into a chain of strange and enchanting events that transforms an ordinary journey underground into an adventure beyond his own time.

Somehow, the routes and spaces of the early Metro become a passage between eras. The doctor crosses into the present day, where he encounters a doctora from contemporary Madrid. Their meeting begins as an impossible collision of two lives separated by more than a century, yet the mystery surrounding Chamberí gives them a chance to know one another. As they seek to understand how the journey has brought them together—and whether it can happen again—their growing attraction develops into a romance challenged by the distance between their worlds.

Their travels bring encounters, comic complications, and moments of discovery, as the contrast between 1919 and the present reveals both what Madrid has changed and what remains recognisably human. The adventure moves through sharply felt emotions: alegría, tristeza, miedo, enfado, asco and sorpresa. Each turn in the mystery tests the pair’s courage and their willingness to value a connection that neither time nor reason can easily explain. What begins with the historic opening of the Metropolitano becomes an intimate voyage through memory, possibility, and the uncertain choices that shape a life.

The musical centres on love’s capacity to bridge apparently unbridgeable distances. It also celebrates curiosity, emotional self-knowledge, and the idea that what matters most in human existence can be rediscovered through connection with others.

show: Ella era Anita (musical staged at Teatre Condal, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
A young Chita grows up within a Puerto Rican family, where the rhythms and pressures of home shape a girl whose future has not yet found its form. An accident later puts the whole of that career in question, demanding resilience at the very moment it seems to close her possibilities down. From that early turning point, she pushes toward the stage and eventually reaches Broadway, where hard-won opportunity becomes an incandescent professional ascent.

Success, however, does not silence the forces that threaten to confine her. As Chita builds a career in musicals including West Side Story, Chicago, and Kiss of the Spider Woman, the woman behind the public triumph confronts obstacles, solitude, motherhood, and the recurring experience of being overlooked. The show does not present these episodes as a straightforward chronology: Chita’s trajectory is set in dialogue with that of the actress and creator who performs her, until the line between biography and theatrical construction dissolves, allowing the private cost of endurance to emerge alongside the glamour of the spotlight.

The figures Chita has embodied—Anita, Velma, and Aurora—step out of their familiar dramatic worlds to become voices within her. They encourage, provoke, accuse, defend, and test her, serving in turn as angels and demons in a dialogue with the identity she has constructed onstage. Their appearances blur the division between performer and role: Anita’s defiance, Velma’s ruthless self-possession, and Aurora’s vulnerability all reveal aspects of Chita’s own conflicts and desires. As these competing voices gather around her, the story moves between lived experience and theatrical invention, asking which self remains when applause fades and which selves must be summoned to survive.

Ultimately, the musical portrays a woman making a life through discipline, courage, and repeated reinvention. Its themes are female artistic ambition, the unseen sacrifices behind achievement, motherhood and solitude, and the power of performance to both conceal and disclose a person’s deepest self.

show: En Joan sense por i la casa encantada (musical staged at SAT! Sant Andreu Teatre, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Joan faces the impossible task of discovering fear: nothing frightens him—not the dark, strange noises, or the monsters imagined beneath a bed. His family have tried everything and grown increasingly worried by his complete lack of alarm. Hoping that a direct encounter with the uncanny will finally change him, they hire an adventure agency to arrange a terrifying weekend in a casa encantada.

The family arrives expecting scares, but the house offers far more than a harmless test of Joan’s nerves. Fantasmes, monstres and malediccions turn the visit into a lively succession of eerie surprises, musical numbers and dances. A particularly terrifying dinner adds to the festivities, while the family waits to see whether any of the house’s inhabitants or disturbances can finally unsettle Joan. Yet he meets each new fright with the same calm curiosity that has baffled his parents.

The key to the weekend lies beyond the rooms of the house, in its garden. Hidden there is a secret whose discovery will determine whether Joan can truly come to understand fear. As the bizarre events build around him, the adventure becomes not merely a contest of shocks, but a journey toward recognising an emotion he has never known. By the end, the question is no longer simply whether the house can frighten Joan, but what it means to confront the unknown when everyone else expects you to be afraid.

Fear is treated as a natural feeling to be understood rather than merely defeated. Through a playful world of supernatural spectacle, the musical contrasts courage with curiosity, family concern with a child’s independence, and apparent scares with the excitement of discovery.

show: Érase otra vez (musical staged at Teatro Salesianos Estrecho, Madrid)
synopsis:
Vera would rather wear trainers than glass slippers, and she has no intention of waiting for anyone to rescue her. In a kingdom where every girl is handed the same script — be pretty, be patient, be chosen — she keeps insisting that her life is hers to decide, and that a princess does not need a prince to give her story a point.

Pablo is a prince, and his problem is the mirror image of hers. What he wants is to dance, to paint, to act; what the palace wants is a prince who behaves like a prince. The expectations attached to his title leave no room for any of it, and the more he is told what a prince should be, the further he drifts from what he actually is. Help arrives from an unlikely quarter: Inspiración a Domicilio, an inspiration service that turns up at the door of anyone who has run out of it.

Once Vera and Pablo find each other, the two of them stop arguing with their own stories and start arguing with the man who writes them. Míster Cuenta Cuentos has been telling these tales the same way for as long as anyone can remember, and he is not inclined to change. Between songs, comic set pieces and increasingly bold acts of rebellion, the pair set out to prove that a story can be told differently — and that the ending does not have to be the one that was handed down.

The show is a fairy tale rewritten for children who are being handed the old one. It argues, cheerfully and without lecturing, that the roles assigned by gender or by birth are not destinies, and that both the girl who wants to run and the boy who wants to dance are entitled to the story they choose.

show: Espejito, Espejito (musical staged at Espacio Alma, Madrid)
synopsis:
Elena barely looks up from her mobile phone when an unexpected encounter draws her out of everyday life and into a fantastical kingdom. There, a reina malvada is absorbed by a competition of her own making: she no longer wants merely to be the most beautiful, but the most popular, most visible and most constantly connected figure in the realm. Her obsession with attention and social networks turns the enchanted world into a place governed by appearances, rankings and the need to be seen.

Elena is pulled into the queen’s adventure and meets a lively collection of fairy-tale figures whose lives are disrupted by this new fixation. Caperucita arrives with her inseparable lobo, while Cenicienta joins the journey through the kingdom. As the group moves from one comic, chaotic predicament to the next, songs and dances accompany their attempts to understand what is happening and to face the challenges before them. The characters must rely on one another rather than on the image each projects, discovering that courage can mean admitting fear, asking for help and trusting a friend.

What begins as a playful contest over beauty and popularity becomes a journey that shifts Elena’s attention away from her screen and toward the people immediately around her. In the castle’s colourful world, the queen and her companions learn that the things that seem most important on a display or in a public image can conceal insecurity and loneliness. By confronting their own fears and helping each other through the adventure, they find a more meaningful kind of magic beyond the pressure to be constantly connected.

The musical centres on friendship, self-knowledge and the courage to look past appearances. It also contrasts the lure of digital attention with the value of real presence, shared adventure and human connection.

show: Garfio y la isla del tesoro (musical staged at Teatro Olympia, Valencia)
synopsis:
Peter Pan, el Sombrerero Loco and Gretel find the world of fairy tales thrown into alarming disorder: one realm is gripped by a cold fierce enough to freeze thoughts, while another is scorched by unbearable heat. Determined to restore balance, the three companions seek out Merlín, whose wisdom and magical cauldron may reveal a remedy for the spreading crisis. Gazing into the caldero, Merlín discovers that the answer lies inside a chest buried on a faraway island.

Reaching it will require a ship, so Peter Pan, el Sombrerero Loco and Gretel turn to Garfio. Knowing the pirate’s appetite for treasure, they persuade him to join the expedition by claiming that the chest contains immense riches. Garfio sets sail, taking the unlikely band across the sea toward la isla de Robinsón, where danger and wonder await at every turn. The young audience is enlisted as grumetes aboard the pirate vessel, helping the crew through its perilous voyage.

On the island and in the surrounding waters, the travellers confront the Bruja del Mar and her hostile magic, then face Las Sirenitas, whose hypnotic powers threaten to divert them from their mission. Their gravest adversary is Plastiferón, a monster created from the plastic waste humans have thrown into the sea. To continue toward the hidden chest and the solution it promises, Garfio and his companions must overcome fear, temptation and their own conflicting motives, learning to act together rather than pursuing separate goals.

At its heart, the adventure argues that even overwhelming crises demand collective action, courage and hope. By turning environmental destruction into a fantastical menace, it also stresses shared responsibility for protecting the natural world.

show: Gaudí: El Despertar Del Geni (musical staged at Teatre Poliorama, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
A sickly young Antoni Gaudí watches the natural world with an intensity that others mistake for frailty. Confined by childhood rheumatism and set apart from the easy movement of other children, he turns solitude into a private landscape of observation: the curve of a leaf, the persistence of an insect, the shapes concealed in stone, water and living things. Nature becomes both his refuge and his first teacher, inviting him to see that nothing is truly motionless or without meaning.

As Antoni struggles with pain, uncertainty and the sense of being different, imagination offers him a way forward. Ordinary surroundings become sites of invention; forms that seem inert begin to suggest creatures, structures and possibilities. His inner world grows more vivid through fantasy, humour and dreams, while the people around him encounter a boy whose sensitivity cannot be reduced to illness. Rather than yielding to the limits placed upon him, Antoni learns to transform them into a source of attention, curiosity and creative force.

The journey follows the gradual awakening of a singular way of seeing. Friendship, hardship and moments of wonder help Antoni recognise that he can give shape to what he perceives, connecting the patterns of the natural world with a desire to make and imagine. By the end, the quiet, introspective child has not escaped his difficulties so much as incorporated them into the beginnings of a vocation: he has discovered that the world is full of forms waiting to be understood and brought to life.

The musical centres on creativity born from vulnerability, presenting adversity as something that can sharpen rather than extinguish a person’s vision. It also celebrates nature as a living source of knowledge and imagination, urging audiences to look again at the overlooked details around them.

show: Imagilusion (musical staged at Teatro Corfú 7, Alicante)
synopsis:
In this tribute to the Disney canon, Mickey takes the controls of a magical aircraft as its comandante, while Minnie welcomes the passengers aboard and prepares them for a flight in which imagination, rather than any map, determines the route. As the journey begins, the cabin becomes a gateway to a succession of enchanted worlds, carrying its young and adult travellers from one beloved adventure to another. Each landing introduces figures whose hopes, fears and choices give the voyage its momentum: characters from Frozen confront isolation and the power of sisterly love; El Rey León evokes the responsibility of growing into one’s place in the world; and La Bella y la Bestia asks the travellers to look beyond appearances.

The flight continues through the playfulness of Toy Story, where friendship is tested by jealousy, change and the fear of being left behind. Mary Poppins brings her extraordinary sense of possibility, turning ordinary moments into invitations to wonder. In Agrabah, Aladdín’s wishes, disguises and daring reveal that honesty and courage matter more than wealth or spectacle. The route then reaches the ocean with Moana, whose determination to answer the call beyond the horizon shows how self-discovery can become an act of service to one’s community. Finally, the colours, music and family tensions of Encanto invite everyone aboard to recognise that worth does not depend on possessing a special gift.

Rather than remaining separate stops, these encounters join together as one shared journey. Mickey and Minnie guide the passengers home with a fuller sense that magic is created through empathy, bravery, imagination and the willingness to welcome difference.

The musical celebrates family connection, friendship, self-belief and the courage to grow. Its central message is inclusive: every person belongs in the adventure, and every voice can share in its magic.

show: Jurassic Game (musical staged at Teatro Olympia, Valencia)
synopsis:
An 11-year-old boy loses his beloved baby triceratops when sinister characters burst out of a video game and carry the little dinosaur away. Refusing to abandon his precious companion, he joins forces with his father, and the pair are drawn into the game’s fantastical digital world, where every new setting brings another level, mission, obstacle, or opponent.

Their rescue quest becomes a headlong journey through a realm where prehistoric danger collides with storybook fantasy. Towering dinosaurs block their path, demanding courage and quick thinking from the boy and his father. They encounter strange creatures and a princess whose dancing energy makes her an unexpected ally. At the same time, the villains behind the kidnapping press their own plan: they want to dominate the world, and the stolen triceratops is caught up in their attempt to turn the game’s chaos into real power.

To reach the baby triceratops, father and son must keep advancing through the game’s challenges rather than retreating when the dangers become larger and more absurd. They confront enemies, survive clashes with dinosaurs, and seek help wherever they can find it, while the boundaries between player, character, and spectator dissolve. The boy’s dream of restoring his companion becomes the force that holds the adventure together, and each trial tests whether the two can remain brave, inventive, and united long enough to defeat those who have taken the dinosaur.

At its heart, the musical celebrates imagination as a space where fear can be faced through play, music, and shared adventure. It also centres on loyalty, family teamwork, and the determination to protect someone small and vulnerable against overwhelming odds.

show: La Júlia i el tauró (musical staged at Sat!, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
Júlia packs to leave home and study Biologia when she discovers a notebook her mother has slipped into her suitcase. Its pages draw her back seven years, to the summer when, aged ten, she travelled with her parents to the isolated lighthouse of Unst, at the far edge of the Shetland Islands. Her father has been sent there to repair the lighthouse, while her mother, a marine biologist, is pursuing a more elusive task: finding the Greenland shark, a creature believed to live longer than trees, and uncovering the secret of its extraordinary longevity.

At first, the journey unfolds as an adventure shaped by sea air, solitude, and Júlia’s wonder at the strange, vast northern landscape. The lighthouse becomes the family’s temporary home, and Júlia watches her parents at work: her father fixing what is broken and her mother pushing ever farther into her research. Yet the search gradually changes. Her mother’s fierce determination begins to consume her, turning into an obsession that pulls her away from the people beside her. Júlia, who has trusted her parents as steady and invincible guides, must confront the frightening realization that they are vulnerable, fallible people with limits of their own.

Remembering the summer from the threshold of adulthood, Júlia pieces together what happened at Unst and what it taught her about love, fear, and the need to ask others for help. The past does not offer a simple answer, but it gives her a way to understand both her mother and herself before she begins her own journey away from home.

The musical centres on family bonds tested by change, and on the painful moment when a child first sees their parents as imperfect human beings. It treats mental fragility without stigma, while affirming that care, connection, and a supportive network can matter as much as any solitary quest.

show: La Nit del Músic Alt (musical staged at Teatre Grec, Barcelona, Catalan-language production)
synopsis:
The Banda Municipal de Barcelona takes the stage of the Teatre Grec for something that turns out to be neither a concert nor a play but a staged symposium, mounted for a second year running so that no single model of the form can quietly impose itself. Singers, musicians, chorus members and self-appointed authorities take possession of the event, determined to settle a supposedly simple question—where does musical theatre begin, and where do its borders end?

Their inquiry leads them back to ancient Greece and to the scarcely documented figure known in the writings of Sòfocles and Èsquil as ψηλός μουσικός, Psilós Mousikós: “the tall musician.” No one can say whether the name refers to the anonymous artist’s literal height or to a lofty position as a musical director, nor whether that artist was a man or a woman. Yet the assembled experts treat Psilós Mousikós as the person who persuaded Sòfocles and Èsquil to admit music and dance into drama, thereby founding the musical at the same moment that democracy was taking shape.

The symposium refuses to leave that origin safely in the past. Arguments, demonstrations and musical numbers collide as the performers test every possible definition of the form. Ancient traces of song give way to radically different theatrical idioms, and the repertory leaps among composers and traditions: Offenbach, Gershwin, Cole Porter, Kurt Weill, Andrew Lloyd Webber, Carles Santos and Albert Guinovart. Instead of delivering a settled history, the gathering turns each example into evidence for a more expansive, contradictory idea of what a musical can be.

By the end, the tribute to Psilós Mousikós has become a defence of artistic plurality. The show treats musical theatre as a democratic space: one in which music, movement, argument and performance continually challenge any single authority’s attempt to define the genre.

show: La Ópera de los tres centavos, con Coque Malla (musical staged at Teatro Infanta Isabel, Madrid)
synopsis:
Mackie Navaja rules the streets of interwar London through prostitution, bribery and violence, turning crime into a flourishing enterprise beneath the city’s respectable façade. His position seems secure until he secretly marries Polly, the sharp-minded daughter of Jonathan Peachum, a businessman who has made a fortune by organising beggars and profiting from their misery. Polly’s marriage turns a private alliance into a dangerous contest of power: Peachum refuses to let his daughter—and the influence she represents—belong to a criminal beyond his control.

Determined to destroy his new son-in-law, Peachum seeks help from the authorities. Yet Mackie has a powerful protection of his own in Tiger Brown, the police chief and an old friend, whose loyalty initially shields him from arrest. While Mackie continues to move among the city’s brothels, deals and betrayals, Polly proves herself far more than a compliant bride. She understands the machinery of Mackie’s business and is capable of taking her place among the calculating men who try to decide her fate.

Peachum escalates the conflict by mobilising the beggars under his command, threatening disorder that will embarrass the authorities and force them to act. The pressure closes around Mackie as friendships, money and official power prove as unreliable as the criminals who exploit them. He is finally captured, tried and condemned to death. At the brink of execution, however, the Crown grants him an absurd last-minute pardon, transforming a supposedly solemn act of justice into another public performance.

The show portrays a world in which poverty, crime, business and government operate by the same ruthless logic: survival belongs to whoever can exploit another person most effectively. Its bitter comedy exposes corruption, class inequality and the arbitrary nature of justice, while Polly’s manoeuvring challenges the power structures surrounding her.

show: La Rumba (musical staged at Foro Stelaris Fiesta Americana Reforma, Ciudad de México, Mexican production)
synopsis:
Two elderly women slip away from the nursing-home outing that was taking them to see the Ángel de la Independencia. Lost in a city they no longer recognise, they take shelter in an abandoned building — and realise it is the ruined rumba hall where they worked when they were young. Chencha Carmina, once a rumbera, and her inseparable friend Toñita Lelé have walked back into the scene of their old glories, and the faded room immediately stirs the lives they thought had been left behind: the music, the costumes, the applause, and the charged atmosphere of a world in which they were not merely spectators, but stars.

Inside the ruined hall the women retrace the path of their youth, and their younger selves — Carmina and Lelé — take over the stage to play out what happened there. Recollections unfold through songs, dances, jokes, and theatrical turns that bring the golden age of Mexico’s rumberas and vedettes vividly back to life. The return is not entirely gentle. Old rivalries resurface alongside affectionate memories, and the two women confront the hurts, ambitions, jealousies, and dreams that accompanied their shared history onstage. Their reunion turns the abandoned hall into a living performance space, where the two timelines continually overlap.

As they revive familiar routines and face one another without the distance imposed by time, both women rediscover the identities that age and institutional life have threatened to erase. The cabaret becomes a place of liberation: a room in which they can again be extravagant, witty, desired, competitive, vulnerable, and fully alive. Laughter softens the melancholy of what has been lost, while the spectacle’s music and choreography transform remembrance into an act of defiance. Rather than accepting that their best days are over, they claim the right to celebrate them—and to create a final moment of radiance together.

The musical celebrates friendship, memory, and an enduring passion for performance. It suggests that glamour may fade from view, but the inner vitality it awakens does not disappear with age.

show: La vida en un segundo (musical staged at Teatro Arlequín Gran Vía, Madrid)
synopsis:
A single actor plays every character in this story of love, friendship and loss. On New Year’s Eve, Lázaro stands abandoned in the Puerta del Sol after his girlfriend leaves him, the latest blow in a life worn down by years of precarious, dead-end work. Desperate and humiliated while Madrid counts down to midnight, he attempts to swallow the traditional grapes with the clock chimes—and chokes on one. In the instant of his death, time collapses: everything he has been, lost, feared, and left unresolved seems to flash before him.

Instead of finding a simple ending, Lázaro is drawn into an unexpected passage beyond life. The boundary between the familiar world and el otro barrio becomes a comic, emotional space populated by the people and voices that shape his reckoning. As he moves through this strange new territory, he is forced to confront the disappointments that led him to believe he had reached the bottom: the exhaustion of insecure work, the wound of abandonment, and the loneliness hidden beneath everyday survival. His journey continually shifts between absurdity and tenderness, allowing laughter to interrupt grief without erasing it.

Music drives Lázaro through each encounter and emotional turn, turning memories, arguments, doubts, and revelations into a fast-moving inner voyage. The afterlife proves less like a final judgement than a chance to look at his existence from a different distance. What begins with a death that feels ridiculous and cruel gradually becomes an opportunity to reconsider the people he has loved, the friendships that have sustained him, and the possibility that meaning can survive even when the future appears to have vanished.

At its heart, the story is about love, friendship, loss, and the precariousness of ordinary life. It suggests that death may sharpen rather than end one’s awareness of what made life worth living—and that humour can coexist with mourning.

show: Libre (musical staged at Teatro Amaya, Madrid)
synopsis:
At the height of a performance, Nino Bravo’s voice bursts into the spotlight, and the memories around it begin to move. Four performers of Melomans use only their voices to conjure the sound of an entire orchestra, carrying the audience through the swift rise of the Valencian singer whose songs became inseparable from the public’s emotional life. The action shifts between musical numbers, comic sketches and recollections, tracing Nino Bravo not as a distant legend but as a young man whose talent, drive and warmth propel him from early aspirations toward national fame.

As success gathers pace, the show revisits decisive moments in his career and the human anecdotes that sit behind the familiar image. Nino Bravo encounters the pressures, excitement and absurdities of a rapidly expanding public life, while figures such as José María Íñigo, Carmen Sevilla and Lola Flores appear within the company’s playful theatrical evocations. The performers turn interviews, encounters and career milestones into lively scenes, allowing humour to interrupt solemnity and keeping the story close to the affectionate memories of colleagues, friends and family.

His songs continually reshape the narrative: moments of ambition, romance, separation, longing and exhilaration emerge through a repertoire of more than sixty numbers. Rather than presenting a straightforward imitation, the production lets the four voices create its changing worlds through vocal loops, layered harmonies and rhythmic sequences. The journey also makes room for the private man—the friend, companion and father—whose life exists alongside the immense public voice.

Ultimately, Libre is about the meeting of art and memory: how a singer’s voice can preserve feeling across generations. It celebrates affection, companionship, humour and the enduring freedom found in songs that people continue to make their own.

show: Mentidrags (musical staged at Teatro Aldama, México, Mexican production)
synopsis:
At Emmanuel Mijares’s funeral, Daniela, Dulce, Lupita and Yuri arrive expecting to mourn a man each believed was hers alone. The four glamorous women—each armed with a different account of her romance with Emmanuel—are instead forced into the same room by Manoella, the elegant, enigmatic figure who holds the key to the dead man’s final instructions. Emmanuel has left behind a letter declaring that he was murdered and demanding that the women uncover the killer hidden among them.

Shock gives way to rivalry as the mourners discover that Emmanuel sustained four simultaneous love affairs. Daniela, polished and proud, insists on the legitimacy of her bond; Dulce’s sweetness conceals wounded fury; Lupita refuses to be underestimated; and Yuri meets every accusation with theatrical confidence. Their clashing memories reconstruct a maze of dates, gifts, promises, jealous confrontations and carefully maintained alibis. Each revelation makes Emmanuel appear less like an ideal lover and more like a master manipulator who tailored himself to whoever stood before him.

The investigation grows volatile once the women realise that none of them has told the whole truth. Old resentments and private ambitions turn allies into adversaries, while Emmanuel keeps dominating the room through the secrets he left behind. As they revisit the decisive night, the question shifts from who had the strongest motive to whether any of them can be trusted at all.

Every role here is played by a drag performer, in costumes built for this version alone. At its core, the show turns romantic deception into a flamboyant mystery about trust, jealousy and the identities people perform for love. The exaggeration, the costumes and the scenic freedom of drag amplify the humour, the melodrama and the show’s implicit critique of gender roles and romantic expectation, in a version that pays open tribute to the LGBTQ+ audience Mentiras has always had. Its comic excesses expose the cost of believing in a fantasy while celebrating resilience, solidarity and the freedom to reclaim one’s own story.

show: Mi madre, Serrat y yo (musical staged at Artespacio Plot Point, Madrid)
synopsis:
Penélope arrives at Lucía’s door carrying a suitcase, having left José Mari, the pharmacist she married, and needing somewhere to begin again. Lucía—her mother, a writer of children’s stories who has lived in Spain since 1976, met Joan Manuel Serrat in Buenos Aires and has made his songs and outlook part of her everyday life—takes her in, but the reunion quickly turns their home into a battleground of habits, temperaments, and sharply different ideas about how to live.

Penélope teaches singing and directs a choir, yet is convinced her own voice is ugly; orderly and practical, she is intent on putting her life back together and inclined to blame her mother—and Serrat—for how it turned out; Lucía is impulsive, eccentric, and determined to meet each disappointment with humour, music, and emotional candour. Their forced cohabitation releases old frictions as well as fresh embarrassments. Mother and daughter argue, tease one another, and stumble into comic situations, yet neither can entirely conceal how much the other’s judgement and affection matter. Amid the domestic clashes, Penélope must confront the aftermath of her separation and recover confidence in herself rather than merely seek refuge in her mother’s house.

The songs of Serrat become part of their shared language, surfacing between quarrels and confessions to give their experiences new emotional weight. They evoke the women’s desires, regrets, endurance, and capacity for reinvention, while helping Lucía and Penélope speak about feelings they might otherwise leave unsaid. As the relationship shifts from exasperated dependence toward mutual recognition, Penélope finds the courage to step forward—including making her debut as a soloist—while Lucía learns that supporting her daughter sometimes means allowing her to choose her own path.

At its heart, the musical is about the unruly love between mothers and daughters: a bond shaped by conflict, care, memory, and the difficulty of seeing each other as independent people. It also celebrates forgiveness, gratitude, resilience after heartbreak, and the possibility of beginning anew at any age.

show: Mi Padre, Sabina y Yo (musical staged at Artespacio Plot Point, Madrid)
synopsis:
This is not a musical in the usual sense but a play carried by songs, in which Joaquín’s idol, muse and imaginary guide is Joaquín Sabina himself. On 28 December the doorbell cuts through one of Joaquín’s habitual parties: amid the women, drink, noise and rock-and-roll excess, a 25-year-old stranger named Jaime stands outside claiming to be his son. Jaime, a singer still bruised by the end of a relationship and unsure of where his life is heading, has tracked down the man he believes to be his father. Joaquín is a celebrated three-Michelin-star chef, but he is also an irrepressible womanizer: charming, reckless, determined to remain young, and used to arranging his life around pleasure rather than responsibility. Jaime refuses to leave until Joaquín acknowledges him—or until the results of an ADN test settle the question—and the unexpected visitor moves into Joaquín’s home.

The forced arrangement immediately unsettles them both. Jaime’s innocence, caution and comparatively orderly habits clash with Joaquín’s unruly existence, while Joaquín’s bravado and appetite for risk challenge the young man’s idealized notions of adulthood and fatherhood. Their arguments expose mutual vulnerabilities: Jaime’s need to belong and to find direction, and Joaquín’s fear of age, commitment and the consequences of the life he has chosen. As their days together unfold, flashbacks illuminate the emotional routes that brought them to this confrontation, while songs shape the shifts between comic chaos, confrontation and moments of unexpected tenderness.

Waiting for the ADN results becomes more than a practical delay. Jaime and Joaquín trade advice, irritate one another, test boundaries and gradually discover forms of trust neither expected. By the time certainty about their biological connection can arrive, their shared experiences have already begun to create a relationship that feels recognizably like that of father and son.
